entries.clue: Bigwig: most important figure on the board? (1,4,7,3)

annotation.definition2: most important figure on the board

blocks.note: the one everybody in the room defers to

blocks.clueFragment: most important figure on the board
blocks.note: the piece a whole game of chess is played to keep safe, standing among the other pieces

annotation.surface: The most important person sitting round a company's boardroom table.
annotation.walkthrough: Chess pieces are men, which is what lets one of them stand amongst the rest. 'Board' pulls towards the boardroom first, and the top figure there is a chairman.
annotation.definitionFit: The phrase is the idiom for somebody head and shoulders above everyone around, and on a chessboard the same words are literal: one figure outranks all the other men.

entries.clue: A cow's audible 'Hello' (5)

indicatorNotes.audible: What is audible is heard rather than read, so the words are worth their sound and not their spelling.

blocks.note: cattle low, so a cow is a lower, and the two words run together into the greeting

annotation.surface: A cow calling out a greeting loudly enough to be heard.
annotation.walkthrough: To low is to make the noise cattle make, which turns a cow into a lower. The trap is reading 'cow's' as a possessive and hunting for something the animal owns.
annotation.definitionFit: Aloha is the Hawaiian word of welcome, handed out with a garland at the airport, and it serves for goodbye as well.

entries.clue: Learned but not liberal - say again? (7)

indicatorNotes.but not: 'But not' rules out what follows it, so the letter named there is struck from the letters already found.

blocks.note: a learned person is literate
l is the standard abbreviation for liberal, and it is the letter that goes

annotation.surface: A well-read person who is anything but liberal.
annotation.walkthrough: Learned is the adjective here, two syllables, meaning scholarly rather than the past tense of learn. The italics on 'not' are the setter flagging that a word is an instruction.
annotation.definitionFit: To iterate is to say a thing over again — the verb inside 'reiterate' and inside the repeated loops of computing.

entries.clue: One seeking riches, gross, grasping: worn-out and explosive (4,5)

indicatorNotes.grasping: Something grasping closes its hands round what is next to it, so the letters named after it go inside the ones named before.

blocks.note: gr is the short form of gross, the dozen dozen
anything worn-out is old
a mine is the explosive buried in the ground or moored at sea

annotation.surface: A coarse, greedy fortune-hunter, worn out and ready to go off at anyone.
annotation.walkthrough: Gross is the dozen dozen, 144, and gr is how a stock list writes it — nothing to do with being coarse. Both halves of the answer sit in the surface disguised as a man's character.
annotation.definitionFit: A gold miner works a seam in the hope of striking it rich, so seeking riches is the whole of the job.

entries.clue: Small, English: Englishman in Oz, when rebuffed, sulks (5)

indicatorNotes.when rebuffed: To be rebuffed is to be turned back, so everything collected up to that point is written out the other way round.

blocks.note: s = small, the label in the neck of a shirt
e is the standard abbreviation for English
pom is what Australians call an Englishman

annotation.surface: A small Englishman snubbed down under and left feeling sorry for himself.
annotation.walkthrough: Oz is Australia, and a pom is what Australians have called the English since the First World War. Three separate pieces go in and all of them come out backwards, which is why the two abbreviations finish at the end.
annotation.definitionFit: Someone who mopes goes about listless and silent over something, which is sulking with the temper left out.

entries.clue: Such as the Round Table, you say, or such as the Hippodrome? (9)

indicatorNotes.you say: 'You say' points at the spoken version of the words, so what is wanted is the spelling you would write down on hearing them.

blocks.note: the Round Table was the club King Arthur's knights belonged to, and a knight club is heard as one word

annotation.surface: Arthur's Round Table and a famous London venue offered as the same sort of thing.
annotation.walkthrough: The Hippodrome in Leicester Square has been a circus, a theatre and a casino, and is best known now for its late nights. Knight loses only its silent k on the way across.
annotation.definitionFit: The Hippodrome is a London venue that trades as a nightclub, so the clue defines by naming one example of the thing.

entries.clue: Quiet little fellow, singleton left here (5)

annotation.definitionNote: The definition points rather than names: 'here' is the place in the idiom about being left unmarried, and the answer is the place it means.

blocks.note: sh is what you say to hush somebody
an elf is the small fellow of folklore

annotation.surface: A quiet little chap, unattached, left standing where he is.
annotation.walkthrough: Left on the shelf is the old British phrase for staying unmarried, said of goods nobody takes down. Sh for quiet and elf for a small fellow are two of the most used pieces in the business.
annotation.definitionFit: The shelf is where the idiom puts anyone nobody has married, which is exactly where the clue's singleton is left.

entries.clue: Megabucks are invested in tower (7)

indicatorNotes.invested in: To invest in something is to put money into it, and putting one thing into another is what the word does to the letters here.

blocks.note: a mint is a fortune — it cost a mint — as well as the place money is struck
the little word is taken as it stands

annotation.surface: A fortune being sunk into the building of a tower.
annotation.walkthrough: A minaret is the slender tower of a mosque, the one the call to prayer goes out from. 'Are' does nothing at all in the surface except carry its own three letters.
annotation.definitionFit: A minaret is the tall thin tower attached to a mosque, so the definition names it flatly.

entries.clue: The sonar acting up in arm of Atlantic (5,3)

indicatorNotes.acting up: Equipment acting up is not behaving as it should, and letters that misbehave will not stay in the order they were given.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, eight letters
anagram indicator

annotation.surface: A ship's sonar playing up in the waters off the Atlantic.
annotation.walkthrough: Sonar belongs so naturally at sea that the first two words read as scenery rather than as eight letters to shuffle. The North Sea is the shallow shelf water between Britain and Norway.
annotation.definitionFit: The North Sea opens into the Atlantic round the top of Scotland, which makes it one of that ocean's arms rather than a sea in its own right.

entries.clue: Drink too much? Coincidence! (7)

blocks.note: over- is the prefix English puts in front of a verb to say too much of it
to lap is to drink with the tongue, the way a cat does

annotation.surface: Somebody waving away a question about their drinking as pure chance.
annotation.walkthrough: The prefix goes in front, so the two pieces land the opposite way round from the clue: to drink too much is to over-lap. Lap is the cat's way of taking water.
annotation.definitionFit: An overlap is the stretch two things share, so events falling across the same span of time meet there — which is what a coincidence is.

entries.clue: Frenchman given tiny bit of work; in retrospect, increasingly naive (7)

indicatorNotes.in retrospect: To look at something in retrospect is to look back over it, so the letters are read from the far end towards the front.

blocks.note: René is a common French given name and the crossword's stock Frenchman
an erg is the physicist's unit of work, and a very small one

annotation.surface: A Frenchman handed a scrap of a job, looking back on it afterwards.
annotation.walkthrough: An erg is the unit of work in the old cgs system, small enough that lifting a grain of rice spends a few hundred of them. Green for inexperienced is the green of a greenhorn.
annotation.definitionFit: Green is the colour English gives to inexperience, so someone greener than the next person is the more easily taken in.

entries.clue: Territorial Army hiding rattle (5)

indicatorNotes.hiding: Something hiding is in the room but covered over, so the letters sit unbroken inside the words in front of you.

blocks.note: five letters running from the end of the first word into the start of the second

annotation.surface: The Territorial Army keeping something quiet.
annotation.walkthrough: The Territorial Army was Britain's part-time volunteer reserve, renamed the Army Reserve in 2014. 'Rattle' offers a baby's toy and means the verb.
annotation.definitionFit: To rattle a person is to shake their composure, which is what alarming them does.

entries.clue: Leaves presents (4,5)

blocks.note: departs, as a train leaves a platform
lays something out in full for others to consider

annotation.surface: Somebody leaving gifts behind them.
annotation.walkthrough: Two words, and the surface makes the second a pile of parcels when it is a verb like the first. A case is set forth in a document; a traveller sets forth at dawn.
annotation.definitionFit: To set forth is to start out on a journey and also to lay an argument out point by point, which is what presenting it amounts to.

entries.clue: Philosopher twisting jar seal: peanut butter at last! (4-4,6)

indicatorNotes.twisting: Twisting something pulls it out of shape, so the letters beside the word come out in an order of their own.
indicatorNotes.at last: At last points to the end of the word next to it, so only its final letter is taken.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, thirteen letters
the final letter of butter, joining the fodder
anagram indicator

annotation.surface: A jar of peanut butter whose seal finally gives when you twist it.
annotation.walkthrough: Everything after the first word belongs in the kitchen, which is what keeps 'Philosopher' looking like part of the story instead of the definition. Fourteen letters, and one has to be fetched from the end of butter.
annotation.definitionFit: Jean-Paul Sartre was the French existentialist who wrote Being and Nothingness and turned the Nobel Prize down, so philosopher was his trade.

entries.clue: Some creamer I can order for coffee (9)

indicatorNotes.Some: 'Some' asks for a part and not the whole, so a run of letters is taken out of the words as they already stand.

blocks.note: nine letters running straight on, from the middle of creamer to the first letter of order

annotation.surface: Checking which of the creamers on offer can be ordered with a coffee.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Order' looks like an instruction to rearrange and is really the last letter of the run. An americano is espresso let down with hot water, said to have been mixed for American soldiers in Italy who found espresso too fierce.
annotation.definitionFit: An americano is a coffee, espresso with hot water added, so the definition simply names the family it belongs to.

entries.clue: Professed nuance; don dubious (9)

indicatorNotes.dubious: What is dubious cannot be trusted, and letters that cannot be trusted will not stay as they were written.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, nine letters
anagram indicator

annotation.surface: A don of questionable standing casting doubt on a fine distinction.
annotation.walkthrough: Professed is a past tense here, meaning declared openly, not the academic word the don in the surface is steering you towards. Three ns in nine letters is the tell once you count them.
annotation.definitionFit: To profess a thing is to declare it openly, which is what announcing it does — the claim is made where everyone can hear.

entries.clue: One shooting around outstripped hare, backing over - primarily, this one's charged to protect (8)

annotation.definition: One shooting around outstripped hare, backing over

indicatorNotes.primarily: Primarily means first of all, so each word it governs hands over the letter it begins with.
indicatorNotes.to protect: Protecting something means getting round the outside of it, so one set of letters closes over the others.

blocks.note: to charge off somewhere is to tear off — he tore down the road
the opening letters of the two words, in order
the apostrophe-s is short for is

annotation.surface: A gunman who has outrun a hare and is under orders to guard somebody.
annotation.walkthrough: The definition is the whole first half, and it is deadpan: Aesop's plodder does no shooting around and still finishes ahead. Its backing is the shell. 'Charged' is the hard word, and it means tore.
annotation.definitionFit: In Aesop's fable the tortoise outstrips the hare by never stopping, and it carries its backing — the shell — over itself the whole way.

entries.clue: Fruity character you might pull in the pub (3-5,6)

annotation.definition: Fruity character you might pull in the pub

blocks.note: read as a colourful eccentric propping up the bar, and meant as the machine that pays out when its cherries and lemons line up

blocks.clueFragment: you might pull in the pub
blocks.note: read as getting off with somebody on a night out, and meant as hauling down the single lever on the machine's side

annotation.surface: A colourful eccentric in the bar, the sort you might get talking to on a night out.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Pull' is British for getting off with somebody, which is the reading the pub pushes. A fruit machine is named for the cherries and lemons on its reels, and the old ones were worked by a lever on the side.
annotation.definitionFit: A one-armed bandit is the fruit machine in the corner of a British pub: one lever for an arm, and a bandit because it takes your money.

entries.clue: Not a good look! (4,3)

blocks.note: what is not good is evil
an eye is a look — to give somebody the eye

annotation.surface: A verdict on somebody's unflattering outfit.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Not a good look' is the modern phrase for behaviour that reflects badly on you, and that is all the surface is doing. The evil eye is the stare superstition says will curse whoever it lands on.
annotation.definitionFit: The whole clue reads straight: the evil eye is a look, and a look cast to do harm is not a good one.

entries.clue: Everyman to ultimate degree - routine, overwhelmed, to be honest (2,5)

indicatorNotes.overwhelmed: To be overwhelmed is to be covered over completely, so those letters end up buried inside the letters around them.

blocks.note: Everyman is the setter of this puzzle, and a setter speaking of themselves is i
to the nth degree is the phrase for taken as far as a thing can go
a rut is the routine somebody gets stuck in

annotation.surface: Everyman, pushed to the limit and buried in routine, owns up to how things stand.
annotation.walkthrough: To the nth degree is the mathematician's way of saying as far as anything can go, and it is sitting almost unaltered in the clue. Setters write themselves as i, and this one signs as Everyman.
annotation.definitionFit: In truth prefaces a candid admission — in truth, I never liked it — which is the job 'to be honest' does in conversation.

entries.clue: Visibly edgy, getting tense before spelling (9)

blocks.note: t = tense, the grammar book's abbreviation
spelling here is casting spells, which is witching

annotation.surface: Somebody getting nervous in the minutes before a spelling test.
annotation.walkthrough: The spelling is the witch's kind, from the same root as bewitch, not the classroom's. 'Tense' works twice over: an adjective in the surface, a grammatical term in the wordplay.
annotation.definitionFit: Somebody twitching cannot hold still, and the small involuntary jerks are nerves anybody in the room can see.

entries.clue: Spiteful, like an Abyssinian (5)

blocks.note: mean in a small, personal, gossiping way
an Abyssinian is a breed of domestic cat, so anything resembling one resembles a cat

annotation.surface: Somebody's spite compared to the temper of an Ethiopian.
annotation.walkthrough: Abyssinia is the old name for Ethiopia, which is the reading the surface wants; the answer needs the cat breed that carries the same name. The spite is the gossiping sort, not the violent sort.
annotation.definitionFit: Catty means spiteful in a sly, small-scale way, and an Abyssinian is a breed of domestic cat, so anything like one is catty in the plain sense too.

entries.clue: 'Gold' here, also named 'Ashanti', originally? (5)

indicatorNotes.originally: Originally asks for what came first, and what comes first in a written word is the letter it opens with.

blocks.note: the opening letters of the five words, taken in order

annotation.surface: A place that went by Gold once, and by Ashanti too, in its earliest days.
annotation.walkthrough: The country was the Gold Coast under British rule and took in the old Ashanti kingdom before that, so both names in the clue were once its own. Each word describes the place and surrenders its first letter at the same time.
annotation.definitionFit: The whole clue reads straight: this is the country that was called Gold, that was also named for the Ashanti, and both names came first.

entries.clue: Before 1 in Paris, terribly intricate lunch's starters (5)

indicatorNotes.starters: Starters are what come first at a table, and what comes first in a word is the letter it starts with.

blocks.note: un is French for one, the numeral as a Parisian says it
the opening letters of the three words, in order

annotation.surface: In Paris before one o'clock, the first course of a fearfully elaborate lunch.
annotation.walkthrough: The setter writes 1 as a numeral so it can be the hour in the surface and the French word in the wordplay. 'Terribly' looks like an instruction to shuffle and is there for its t alone.
annotation.definitionFit: Both words fix the far end of a stretch of time: not before Friday and not until Friday put the same limit on it.

entries.clue: Divulge student passed back note (3,2)

indicatorNotes.passed back: Anything passed back travels the way it came, so the word beside it is written out in reverse.

blocks.note: l is the plate a British learner driver carries, and the crossword's standard student
the four letters of note, set down from the back

annotation.surface: A pupil handing a scribbled note back down the row.
annotation.walkthrough: Reversing the note gives a famous English school, and the eye is happy to read the five letters that way rather than as two words. L for learner comes from the plate on a British learner driver's car.
annotation.definitionFit: To let on is to give away something you were supposed to keep to yourself, which is divulging it.

entries.clue: Passivity fashionable, it falls back in time (7)

indicatorNotes.falls back: What falls back drops away the way it came, so those letters are set down in reverse.
indicatorNotes.in: 'In' means within, so the piece named before it goes inside the piece named after.

blocks.note: in = fashionable, as in the in crowd
an era is a stretch of time
the word it, turned round

annotation.surface: Doing nothing is in vogue, and in time the fashion for it falls away.
annotation.walkthrough: 'It' stands for nothing at all — the two letters of the word itself are what is wanted. Era is the crossword's usual 'time', and the comma after the first word is the only sign the definition stops there.
annotation.definitionFit: Inertia is the tendency to stay exactly as you are, which in a person reads as passivity — the refusal to be stirred into anything.

entries.clue: Bill's story (7)

blocks.note: the piece of paper totting up what is owed
the telling of what happened

annotation.surface: A man called Bill and the tale he has to tell.
annotation.walkthrough: Bill takes a capital because it opens the clue, not because it is anybody's name — it is the restaurant kind. The same double runs through settling one and giving one of yourself.
annotation.definitionFit: An account is the bill a shop or a hotel presents, and equally the telling of events — by all accounts, an account of the meeting.

entries.clue: Very tanned, he won sports occasionally (5,3,3,4)

indicatorNotes.sports: A sport is a plant or animal that has come out unlike its parents, so to sport is to turn up in a different form from the one given.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, fifteen letters
anagram indicator

annotation.surface: A deeply suntanned man who picks up the odd win at the athletics.
annotation.walkthrough: A sport in the gardener's sense is a shoot that comes out unlike the plant it grew on, which is how the word comes to mean rearranged. Fifteen letters is a long shuffle, so count them before starting.
annotation.definitionFit: Every now and then describes something that happens at scattered intervals rather than steadily, which is what occasionally says in one word.
